turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got a free weekend and I want to start a new game.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fun. Are you in the mood for a big story you can sink into, or something quick you can pick up and put down?

contexts.pending: a big story game or something quick
think_reask: So, a big story to sink into, or something quick and casual?
Time's up. What are you feeling for the weekend, long story or short sessions?
welcome_back: Welcome back. You were picking a game for the weekend, big story or something quick?
Hi again. Still deciding between an epic and something you can dip in and out of?

endings.user: Big story. I want to disappear for two days.
endings.moshi: Then go for a long open-world adventure. Stock up on snacks first.

endings.user: Something quick. I'll be in and out all weekend.
endings.moshi: A roguelike or a puzzle game would suit you, short runs that still feel satisfying.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My daughter wants a games console for her birthday.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely. Does she mostly want to play on the TV with the family, or carry it around and play on her own?

contexts.pending: family TV console or a handheld for her
think_reask: So, a console for the TV with everyone, or a handheld she can take around?
Okay, what do you think she'd use more, a family console or a portable one?
welcome_back: Welcome back. We were choosing a console for your daughter, TV or portable?
There you are. Have you thought about whether she'd want it for the TV or on the go?

endings.user: Portable, definitely. She'd want it in the car and at her grandma's.
endings.moshi: Then a handheld is perfect. Get a case for it, they get dropped a lot.

endings.user: The TV. Honestly I want to play with her too.
endings.moshi: That's sweet. Pick one with good local multiplayer and grab a second controller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep dying at the same boss and I'm about to give up.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Frustrating. Do you want some tips on beating it, or would you rather turn the difficulty down and enjoy the story?

contexts.pending: boss tips or lowering the difficulty
think_reask: So, do you want tips for the boss, or just lower the difficulty?
Alright, push through with some tips, or make it easier?
welcome_back: Welcome back. You were stuck on that boss. Tips, or turn the difficulty down?
Hi again. Decided how to handle that boss yet?

endings.user: Give me tips. I'm too stubborn to lower it.
endings.moshi: Okay. Spend a few tries just dodging and learning its patterns, without attacking at all.

endings.user: Lower it. I just want to see what happens next.
endings.moshi: No shame in that. You can always turn it back up for the next chapter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I haven't played anything in ten years, but my new job pays well and I miss it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Nice, a comeback. Are you thinking of a gaming PC at your desk, or a console on the big TV in the living room?

think_reask: So, the comeback setup. PC at the desk, or console on the sofa?
Desk or sofa? PC or console?
welcome_back: Your return to gaming. Leaning towards a PC or a console?
So, a PC, or a console under the telly?

endings.user: Console. I stare at a monitor all day at work already.
endings.moshi: Makes total sense. Sofa, big screen, no fiddling with drivers.

endings.user: PC, I think. I want to play the strategy stuff I used to love.
endings.moshi: Good call, strategy games really shine with a mouse and keyboard.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm making my character in this new fantasy game.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The best part. Any idea what you'll play?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's between a sneaky archer and a huge knight in armour.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very different styles. Do you like picking enemies off quietly from far away, or charging straight into the fight?

think_reask: Character time. Archer in the shadows, or knight in the thick of it?
So, sneaky archer or big tanky knight?
welcome_back: Your character's still waiting. Archer or knight?
The character screen. Did you pick between the archer and the knight?

endings.user: Knight. I'm too impatient for sneaking.
endings.moshi: Ha, fair. Put your first points into health and enjoy smashing things.

endings.user: The archer. I love clearing a camp before anyone notices me.
endings.moshi: Great fit. Look for a quiet bow and boots early on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm organising a remote game night for my team at work. About eight people.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fun team bonding. Do you want a silly party game where people compete, or a co-op one where everyone works together?

contexts.pending: competitive party game or co-op game for the team
think_reask: Team game night. Party game chaos, or everyone on the same side?
So, competitive or co-op for your coworkers?
welcome_back: The work game night. Competitive or co-op?
Your team's game night. Were you going for a party game or a co-op one?

endings.user: Party game. A bit of friendly rivalry is good for them.
endings.moshi: Love it. Pick one that runs in a browser so nobody has to install anything.

endings.user: Co-op. Some of them get way too competitive.
endings.moshi: Wise. A co-op puzzle or a shared drawing game keeps it friendly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My eight year old spent forty pounds on in-game coins on my tablet. He didn't realise it was real money.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Oh no, that's really common. Do you want to try asking the store for a refund, or treat it as a lesson and just lock purchases from now on?

contexts.pending: ask for a refund or let it go and lock purchases
think_reask: The forty pounds. Going after a refund, or letting it go?
So, refund request, or chalk it up and lock everything?
welcome_back: Your son's coin spree. Refund, or just lock it down?
The in-game purchase. Are you asking for the money back?

endings.user: I'll ask for a refund. Forty pounds is forty pounds.
endings.moshi: Fair. Explain it was a child's accidental purchase, stores often approve those the first time.

endings.user: I'll let it go and set up a password. He's already very sorry.
endings.moshi: That's kind. Turn on purchase approval in the settings and it can't happen again.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The game just asked me to name my village and I've been staring at the box for five minutes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Naming things is hard! Do you want something funny you'll laugh at every time, or something grand and epic?

think_reask: The village name. Silly, or epic?
That empty name box. Funny or grand?
welcome_back: Your village still needs a name. Funny or epic?
So, the village name. Going silly or serious?

endings.user: Funny. I'm calling it Puddleton.
endings.moshi: Puddleton is perfect. It sounds damp and charming.

endings.user: Epic. Something like Stormhold.
endings.moshi: Stormhold has real weight. Your villagers will feel very brave.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Preorders open tonight for the sequel I've been waiting for.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exciting. Are you getting the standard edition, or splashing out on the collector's box with the statue and art book?

think_reask: Preorder decision. Standard, or the big collector's box?
So, just the game, or the statue and the art book too?
welcome_back: The sequel preorder. Standard or collector's?
So, which edition are you going for?

endings.user: Standard. I don't have shelf space for a statue.
endings.moshi: Totally fair. You'll have the same game and a lot more money.

endings.user: Collector's. I've waited six years, I'm treating myself.
endings.moshi: Then enjoy it. Set an alarm, those sell out fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My wrist has been aching after long gaming sessions.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sorry to hear that. Does it hurt during the day too, or only after playing?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly after. It's getting worse.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then let's act on it. A full week off to rest it, or shorter sessions with breaks?

contexts.pending: a week off or shorter sessions
think_reask: About your wrist. A week off, or shorter sessions?
So, full rest for your wrist, or play less at a time?
welcome_back: Your aching wrist. Rest it completely, or cut down the sessions?
The wrist. Leaning towards a break or shorter sessions?

endings.user: A full week off. It's scaring me a bit.
endings.moshi: Good choice. If it still hurts after the week, see a doctor or physio.

endings.user: Shorter sessions. Maybe forty minutes and then a stretch.
endings.moshi: That's a solid plan. Setting a timer really helps you stick to it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm at the big choice in this story game. The traitor's on his knees begging.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ooh, tense. Are you going to spare him and hope he redeems himself, or banish him from the kingdom for good?

think_reask: The traitor's still kneeling there. Spare him or banish him?
So, mercy or exile?
welcome_back: That traitor. Mercy, or out of the kingdom?
The big choice. Did you settle what happens to him?

endings.user: I'll spare him. Everyone deserves a second chance.
endings.moshi: Merciful. Just keep an eye on him in the next chapter.

endings.user: Banish him. He let my whole party die.
endings.moshi: Hard to argue with that. The kingdom will feel safer, at least.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to start streaming on weekends, just for fun.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds great. For your very first stream, would you play something scary where viewers love watching you jump, or something cozy where you can chat the whole time?

contexts.pending: horror game or cozy game for the first stream
think_reask: First stream. Horror and screaming, or cozy and chatty?
So, scary game, or relaxed one?
welcome_back: Your first stream. Something scary, or something cozy?
The stream. Did you pick the scary game or the chill one?

endings.user: Horror. My friends will love seeing me panic.
endings.moshi: Perfect stream material. Turn your microphone down a bit for the screams.

endings.user: Cozy. I'm nervous, and talking will be easier.
endings.moshi: Smart start. A relaxed game takes the pressure off while you learn the setup.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: {friend}, are you still playing that farming game?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Every night. I'm in my third year now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it worth getting? It looks kind of slow.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: It is slow. That's the point. It's relaxing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can we play it together or is it single player?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: You can do co-op. Get it and I'll show you around my farm.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Did you take my controller again?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Mine ran out of battery. I'll give it back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: You said that yesterday.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Okay, okay. It's on the couch, under the blanket.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the charger?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: No idea. Probably in your room, honestly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: {friend}, do you want to do the raid tonight?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: What time? I've got work early tomorrow.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like eight? It should only take a couple of hours.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Last time you said that we finished at one in the morning.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That was because the tank kept disconnecting. We've got a new one now.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Fine. Eight, and I'm out by ten whatever happens.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Deal. I'll send everyone a message.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Did you finish it last night?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Yeah, and that ending, I can't believe the captain was the one who

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Stop! Don't! I'm two hours from the end!

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Oh no. Did I just ruin it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: You said the captain. Now I'll be suspicious of him the whole time.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Maybe I'm bluffing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are you bluffing?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: I'm not saying anything else. Go play it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: {friend}, the guy downstairs is selling his old console. Two controllers and five games.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: How much does he want?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A hundred and twenty. Is that a good deal?

turns.text: Depends which games. And check the disc drive actually works.

turns.text: Good point. Would you come with me to look at it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why are you holding my controller like that?

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: I need a favour. There's this level with the moving platforms, I've died about fifty times.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: You want me to beat it for you?

turns.speaker: friend

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you recommend a game I could play with my partner? She doesn't really play games.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Co-op puzzle games are great for that. There are lovely ones where you each control a character and have to work together.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She gets stressed with anything / too fast.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then avoid anything with timers. A cozy building or cooking game where nobody can really lose might suit her better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cooking games are chaotic though, aren't they?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some are very chaotic, yes. Look for a relaxed one, or a point and click adventure where you solve things at your own pace.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Point and click sounds good. We could just chat while we play.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. It's more like reading a story together than playing a game.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How many hours of gaming a day is okay for a twelve year old?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There's no magic number, but many parents aim for about an hour or two on school days, a bit more on weekends.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He'd play all day if I let him.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most kids would. It helps to agree on rules together, so it feels less like a punishment.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if he's in the middle of a match when time's up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give a warning about ten minutes before, so he can finish the round. Cutting off a match mid game usually causes a fight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That makes sense. I've been / just turning it off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of parents do. The warning tends to make the whole thing much calmer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it worth upgrading to the new console or should I wait?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on what you play. Are there games coming out that only run on the new one?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Not really. I mostly play older stuff.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then I'd wait. Prices usually drop after the first year or so, and more games come out for it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, but my current one is / getting really loud.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's often just dust in the fan. Cleaning the vents with compressed air can make a big difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've literally never cleaned it. It's eight years old.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's definitely worth a try first. It might buy you another year or two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandson keeps talking about some building game with blocks. What is it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: He probably means a sandbox game where you build anything you like out of blocks, a bit like digital Lego. It's hugely popular with kids.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it violent at all?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very mildly. There are a few cartoon monsters at night, but there's also a mode with no monsters, just building.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I play it with him? I'm seventy-three and / hopeless with computers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You definitely could. Ask him to teach you, kids love being the expert and the basics are simple.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lovely idea. He'd think it was hilarious.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: He'd probably build you a house on the first day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got a long haul flight next week, eleven hours. What should I put on my handheld?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Eleven hours is a lot of time. I'd bring one big game you can sink into and a few short ones for when you're tired.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What counts as a big one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A long role playing game or an open world adventure. Just make sure it works offline, a lot of games need internet these days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, I didn't think of that. / Plane wifi is useless.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Download everything and launch each game once at home to check. Some need updates the first time you open them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And battery?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bring a power bank and lower the screen brightness. Turn on flight mode on the handheld too, it saves a surprising amount of charge.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My daughter wants to play online with her friends. She's ten and I'm nervous about strangers talking to her.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a very reasonable worry. Most consoles have parental controls that let you limit chat to friends you approve.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So she can play with her school friends but not randoms?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. You can usually set it so only friends can message or voice chat. Some games also have their own chat settings, so check those too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if someone is / nasty to her anyway?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Teach her how to block and report, and make sure she knows she can tell you without getting in trouble. That last part matters most.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I sit with her?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: At first, it's a nice idea. Keeping the console in a shared room, like the living room, makes it easy to keep an eye on things without hovering.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm stuck on a puzzle in this temple and I don't want a full walkthrough, just a nudge.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I like that approach. Tell me what the room looks like and what you've tried.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There are four statues that rotate and a door with a symbol of a sun.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Okay, without spoiling it. Look closely at what the statues are holding or facing. Is there anything in the room that relates to the sun?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a window. Light comes in / at an angle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a big clue. Think about what would happen if something blocked or reflected that light.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh. Oh! The statue with the shield.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds like you're onto it. I'll stay quiet and let you enjoy solving it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm a student and I want to build my first gaming PC. My budget is tiny.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Doable. The trick on a tight budget is putting most of the money into the graphics card, since that matters most for games.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about everything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A mid range processor is plenty. Sixteen gigabytes of memory, and a solid state drive so games load fast. Don't overspend on a fancy case.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is used stuff a good idea?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Used graphics cards can be great value, just buy from someone with good feedback and test it if you can. I'd buy the power supply new though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why the power supply?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A cheap or worn out one can fail and take other parts with it. It's not exciting, but it protects everything else.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I'm slightly / terrified of putting it together.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most people are the first time. Follow a video slowly, and it's really just careful Lego.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why do first person games make me feel sick? My friends play them for hours.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's called motion sickness, and it's really common. Your eyes see movement but your body is sitting still, and your brain gets confused.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there anything I can do or / am I just doomed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not doomed. Try increasing the field of view in the settings, so you see more of the world around you. That helps a lot of people.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a setting for that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually, yes. Turning off motion blur and camera shake helps too. Some games also let you add a little dot in the centre of the screen.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A dot? That sounds silly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It sounds silly, but it gives your eyes a fixed point. Also play in a bright room, sit a bit further from the screen, and take breaks before you feel bad.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I found a box of my old game cartridges in my mum's loft. Are they worth anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some can be! It depends on the console, which games, and their condition. Do you still have the boxes and manuals?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A few have boxes. Most are just the cartridges.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Loose cartridges of common games usually sell for a little. Rare titles or complete boxed ones can be worth a lot more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I find out / which ones are rare?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Search for each title with the word sold on auction sites. Sold prices tell you what people actually pay, not what sellers hope for.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I might just keep them, honestly. Nostalgia.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lovely reason too. If you do keep them, store them somewhere dry and cool, not back in a hot loft.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My hands are really small and most controllers feel huge.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's more common than you'd think. Some brands make smaller controllers, and there are compact ones designed for younger players that adults use too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Won't those feel cheap?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some do, but there are decent ones. Try to hold a few in a shop before buying if you can.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about remapping buttons?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great idea. Most consoles let you change which button does what in the accessibility settings, so you can move awkward ones somewhere comfier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I didn't know that existed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's often hidden. It's worth a look, you can even swap the sticks or flip the triggers on some systems.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have low vision and I'd love to get into games but text is always tiny.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of games have improved a lot here. Many have settings to enlarge text and menus, and some add high contrast modes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know before I buy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for accessibility reviews. Some websites and community groups rate games specifically on vision features.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are there consoles with / built in options?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, most modern consoles have system wide zoom, text to speech for menus, and colour filters. You can try them before buying any game.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What kind of games work best for me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Slower paced ones tend to be friendlier, like turn based strategy or adventure games, since you're not racing against the clock.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds like my kind of thing anyway.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you're in luck. There's a lot to explore in those genres.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm picking up a game I stopped playing six months ago and I have no idea what I was doing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Classic. Does the game have a quest log or a journal? That's usually the quickest way to remember your goals.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a journal, but I've forgotten all the controls too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the settings menu, there's often a controls page. Or find a quiet area and just press every button to see what happens.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My inventory is also / a total mess.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then give yourself half an hour of tidying. Sell junk, check your gear, and read the item descriptions again. It helps everything come back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I just restart?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Only if you weren't far in, or didn't enjoy your choices. Otherwise, muddle through for an hour and it usually clicks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a local tournament for a fighting game I love. I want to enter but I'm scared I'll get destroyed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's how almost everyone feels before their first one. Local events are usually very welcoming to newcomers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I lose in the first round?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You might, and that's okay. Most tournaments use double elimination, so you get at least two matches. And people often play casual games all day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I practise anything / specific before?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick one character and learn a few reliable moves really well, rather than a bit of everything. Practise blocking too, beginners forget to defend.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And etiquette?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Shake hands or say good games after a match, bring your own controller if you can, and ask people for tips. Players love talking shop.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I'm signing up tonight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Brilliant. Have fun, and go in to learn, not to win.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My save file got corrupted. Eighty hours. Gone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Oh no, I'm really sorry, that's awful. Before you give up, does the game or console have cloud saves?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't know. I never set anything up.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the console's save data settings. Some systems back up automatically if you have an online subscription. Also check if the game keeps auto saves in separate slots.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's an auto save from / two days ago!

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a huge relief. You'll lose a little, but not eighty hours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I stop this happening again?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Turn on cloud backup if you can, keep a few manual saves in different slots, and avoid switching the console off while it's saving.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Six of us want to play together, but we're on different consoles and two are on PC.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That used to be a nightmare, but crossplay is common now. Lots of games let everyone play together regardless of platform.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do we find ones that support six players?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Search for crossplay games with squad sizes of six or more. Party games, some shooters, and a few survival games handle bigger groups.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Most of us / don't want shooting.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then look at party games with mini games, or a co-op survival game where you build things together. A few social deduction games are great with six too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Social deduction, like finding the traitor?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly that. Lots of lying and accusing your friends. It's very fun with a group that knows each other.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Everyone at school is playing this horror game, but I get scared really easily.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's okay, plenty of people do. You could watch someone else play first, so you know what's coming.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wouldn't that spoil it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little, but it makes it far less scary. Or play it in the daytime with the lights on and someone else in the room.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, my little sister / could be my bodyguard.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect bodyguard. Lowering the volume also helps a lot, a big part of horror games is the sound.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I didn't think of that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And it's fine to just say it's not for you. There are plenty of other games to talk about with your friends.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's speedrunning? My brother keeps watching people finish games in like twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's trying to finish a game as fast as possible. People practise routes, tricks and sometimes glitches to shave off seconds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Glitches? Isn't that cheating?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on the category. Some runs allow any trick the game lets you do, others ban glitches completely. The community sets clear rules.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why would anyone / spend years on that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a lot like a sport. People enjoy mastering something, chasing a personal best, and there's a big friendly community around it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I try it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. Pick a short game you already love, look up the beginner route, and time yourself. Beating your own time is surprisingly addictive.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've always wanted to make my own little game. I can't code at all. Is that hopeless?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not hopeless at all. There are free game engines with visual scripting, where you connect blocks instead of writing code.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should my first game be?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Something tiny. A single screen where you jump over obstacles, or a simple maze. Finishing a small game teaches you more than starting a huge one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I had this / massive idea for a fantasy world though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep that idea in a notebook. Build a few small games first, and you'll have the skills to make that world much better later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long does a tiny game take?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A weekend or two, if you follow a beginner tutorial. Game jams are fun too, people make a game in a few days around a theme.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds terrifying and great.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's exactly the right mix. Have fun with it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friends keep saying my headset mic sounds terrible. Like I'm underwater.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's annoying for everyone. First, is it plugged in through a cable or connected wirelessly?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wireless, through the controller.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the console's audio settings. Sometimes the mic is set to very low quality to save bandwidth, or a monitor setting adds an echo.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There is a / mic level slider.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try lowering the input level a bit. If it's too high, it distorts, which can sound muffled. Also check the mic isn't touching your face or cheek.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It kind of is.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Move it about two fingers' width from your mouth, slightly to the side. That alone often fixes the underwater sound.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My mum's sixty five and just retired. She says she wants to try a video game. Where do I even start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: How lovely. Does she like puzzles, gardening, mysteries? Matching the game to her interests matters more than anything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She does crosswords every single day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then word puzzle games or gentle logic games on a tablet would suit her. Touch controls are much easier than learning a controller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She might like / something with a story too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There are lovely mystery games where you explore a house and solve puzzles at your own pace. Nothing is timed and nothing jumps out at you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I play with her the first time?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, but let her hold the tablet. Show her once, then sit on your hands. People learn much faster when they're the ones tapping.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep saying I'll play one round and then study, and then it's two in the morning.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very human. Games are designed to make one more round feel tempting. Do you want some tricks to break the loop?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Please. My exams are in three weeks.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Flip it around. Study first, and use a game session as the reward. Set a timer on your phone and stop when it goes off, even mid match.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mid match is / brutal though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then pick games without long matches during exam season. Or play only on certain evenings, so you're not deciding every night.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe I'll give my console to my roommate.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Honestly, that works for a lot of people. Out of sight really helps for a few weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: People in my online matches are so rude. Someone just spent the whole game insulting me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's really unpleasant, and it's not your fault. The quickest fix is muting them, you don't owe anyone your attention.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I report them too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, if the game has a report option. It takes a few seconds, and repeated reports do lead to bans in many games.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's making me not / want to play anymore.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's understandable. You could turn off voice chat with strangers and only talk to friends. Text chat can usually be switched off too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then how do I play with a team?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most games have a ping system, where you mark things on the map without talking. Lots of players prefer it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, this is silly, but I've spent four hours just fishing in a huge adventure game.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's not silly at all. Fishing mini games are famously relaxing. What have you caught?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A giant golden carp. I screamed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a proper achievement. Is there a collection or museum in the game where you can show it off?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a fishing log. I've / filled about half.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you've got a whole side quest ahead of you. Some fish only appear at night or in certain weather, so check the times.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I haven't even done the main story.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The story will wait. If you're having fun, you're playing it right.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have about forty games I've bought and never played. How do I even choose?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A classic backlog. One way is to pick by how long they take. Do you want a short win or a long project right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Short. I need to feel like I finish something.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then look up how long each one takes to beat and sort by that. Pick the shortest one you're still curious about.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I don't / like it after an hour?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Drop it, guilt free. A backlog isn't homework. Uninstalling things you won't play makes the list feel lighter too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And stop buying new ones?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That helps. Maybe a rule like finishing one before buying another, at least until the list is a bit friendlier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thinking of buying a VR headset. My living room is pretty small, is that a problem?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends on what you want to play. Many VR games can be played seated or standing in one spot, which needs very little space.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much space for the moving around ones?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Roughly two metres by two metres of clear floor is comfortable. Less than that, and you'll keep bumping the guardian boundary.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have a coffee table / right in the middle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you'd want to push it aside when you play, or stick to seated games. Swinging your arms into a table hurts.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is VR sickness a thing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For some people, yes. Start with short sessions and games where you don't move with a stick, like rhythm games. Most people adjust over a few weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm starting a game everyone says is hard. Should I play on normal, or the easy mode?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally your call. What do you enjoy more, the challenge or the story?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Honestly, both. But I'm a perfectionist, so I hate dying.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then maybe start on normal, and give yourself permission to switch down if it stops being fun. Most games let you change difficulty anytime.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Won't that feel like / I failed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It really shouldn't. The developers added easy mode so more people can enjoy the game. There's no prize for suffering.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Normal, with an escape hatch.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. And if a boss takes you more than an hour, a short break often helps more than anything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My controller's left stick drifts. My character walks off on his own even when I'm not touching it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's stick drift, and it's sadly very common. Is the controller still under warranty?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's about two years old. Probably not.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some manufacturers still repair drift for free, so it's worth checking their support page. If not, you have a few options.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can increase the dead zone in the game settings if it's mild. Some people clean around the stick with a little electronics cleaner. Or you can buy a replacement stick module and swap it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Swap it myself? That sounds / like I'd break it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It involves a tiny screwdriver and sometimes soldering, so it's not for everyone. If you're nervous, a local repair shop can usually do it for less than a new controller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I love the soundtrack of the game I'm playing. I'd like to listen to it while I work.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Game music is great for focus, it's literally designed to sit in the background while you concentrate. Many soundtracks are on music streaming services.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Really? I assumed they weren't.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of them are now, especially from indie studios. Some also sell them directly with bonus tracks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Any others you'd / recommend for working?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for soundtracks from exploration and puzzle games, they tend to be calm and without lyrics. City builders and farming games often have gentle ones too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that a weird thing to do at the office?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not at all. Plenty of people do it. Nobody will know it's from a game unless it suddenly turns into boss battle music.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My girlfriend and I want a cozy game night at home. We've only got one TV.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds lovely. Do you want to work together, or tease each other in a bit of friendly competition?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Together. If I beat her she'll / sulk for an hour.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, co-op it is. There are great split screen puzzle adventures where you each control a character and need each other to progress.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She's never played anything before.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then look for one with simple controls, or a game where one person can take a helper role, like guiding or collecting things.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Snacks and blankets, too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Essential equipment. Maybe agree on a stopping time, those puzzle games can swallow a whole evening.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My two boys fight every evening over whose turn it is on the console.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That sounds exhausting. Would a clear schedule help, so it's not up for debate every night?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We tried that. They argue about the schedule.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try a visual timer they can both see, like a kitchen timer next to the TV. When it rings, it's the timer's fault, not yours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's clever. And if one is / in the middle of a boss fight?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give a five minute warning, and agree that a boss fight can finish, but no starting new levels after the warning.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could they just play together instead?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Absolutely. A couple of co-op games could turn turn taking into teamwork. Not every night, but it might calm things down a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When I play online, everything lags. My character teleports around. Is it my internet?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Possibly. Are you on wifi or plugged into the router with a cable?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wifi. The router is in another room.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's often the culprit. Walls and distance hurt wifi a lot. A cable straight to the console, even a long one, usually fixes most lag.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A long cable across / the hallway though? My flatmate will hate it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fair. Powerline adapters send internet through your home's electrical wiring, so you just plug one near the router and one near the console.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that reliable?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In most homes it works well, and it's usually more stable than wifi. Also check nobody else is streaming or downloading huge files while you play.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got some gift money and I want to pick a new game.
options: The first one is a huge open world fantasy game, like a hundred hours long, with gorgeous graphics.
Then there's a short indie puzzle game, maybe six hours, that everyone says is really clever.
Option three is an online shooter my friends play every night, but it's full of microtransactions.
And the last one is a cozy farming game where you grow crops and decorate a little house.
moshi_comment: If you want to play with your friends, the shooter is the obvious pick, even with the extra purchases. The fantasy game is great value if you have lots of free time. The puzzle game is perfect if you just want something short and satisfying.
How much time do you actually have to play these days? If it's only an hour here and there, the farming game or the puzzle game fit best. The hundred hour one could end up sitting unfinished.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm trying to decide what to play with my little brother this weekend.
options: One is a racing game with silly karts that we can both play on the same screen.
Another is a building game where we make castles and explore caves together.
Or there's a dance game that uses the controllers, which would get us both moving around.
moshi_comment: The kart racer is a classic for siblings, it's quick to pick up and really fun to compete. The building game is better if you'd rather work together than compete. The dance game is great for a laugh but might tire out fast.
How old is your brother? If he's pretty young, the building game is gentler since nobody loses. If he's competitive, the kart racer will be a hit.

option_sets.lead_in: I've saved up enough to upgrade one part of my gaming setup, and I keep changing my mind.
options: A new graphics card would let me play the latest games on high settings, but it's the priciest.
Or a really good monitor, bigger and faster, so everything I already play looks smoother.
I could also get a proper desk chair, because my back hurts after an evening of playing.
And there's a nice wireless headset, which would mean no more tangled cables when I play with friends.
moshi_comment: The graphics card and the monitor both make games look better, but the monitor helps everything you already own. Honestly though, if your back hurts, the chair might matter most. The headset is a nice to have.

I'd think about the chair first, since pain makes every session worse. Between the card and the monitor, the monitor is better value unless your current card struggles. The headset can wait for a birthday.

option_sets.lead_in: My nephew's visiting for a week and I need a game we can both enjoy. He's eleven.
options: There's a co-op platformer where we each play a little robot and help each other across levels.
He's also obsessed with a football game, though I'm terrible at it and he'd crush me.
Or a monster catching adventure on the handheld, which we could each play and then trade.
moshi_comment: The robot platformer is built for exactly this, two people helping each other, so nobody feels left out. The football game might be fun for him but frustrating for you. The monster game works if you like doing your own thing side by side.
I'd go with the co-op platformer. He gets to play with you, not just beat you. The football game is fine for a night or two, and the monster adventure is a nice quiet backup.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got a five hour train ride tomorrow and I want to bring something to play.
options: My handheld has a long role playing game I started months ago and never finished.
There's also a puzzle app on my phone with hundreds of short levels, no internet needed.
I could take my old retro handheld with a few classic platformers, tiny and the battery lasts forever.
Or I bring a book of logic puzzles and a pen and give screens a rest.
moshi_comment: Five hours is a perfect chunk to make real progress on that role playing game, if the battery holds out. The phone puzzles are great as a backup when you're tired. The retro handheld and the logic book are both lovely low battery options.

I'd bring the handheld with the long game and finally get into it, then switch to the phone puzzles. The retro console is fun but you might finish those games fast, and the book is nice if you want a break from screens.

option_sets.lead_in: My friends want to start a weekly game night and asked me to pick what we play.
options: A space survival game where we build a base together and try not to starve.
There's a pirate game where we sail one ship and everybody has a job, steering, sails or cannons.
Or a quick card battler, very competitive, matches only take ten minutes.
moshi_comment: The survival game and the pirate game are both great for a regular group, because there's progress to come back to each week. The pirate one gets chaotic in a fun way. The card battler is better as a warm up than the main event.

For a weekly night, I'd go with the pirate ship. Everyone has a role, and the funniest stories come out of it. The space base is great if your friends like planning, and the card game suits people who only drop in for a bit.
